title: Leukoma Adherent: The Scarred Gateway
summary: A complex clinical entity featuring a dense full-thickness corneal opacity with iris tissue incarcerated or attached to its posterior surface. It represents the end-stage of a corneal perforation, where the iris acts as a natural tamponade.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Leukoma Adherent is a dense, white, vascularized or non-vascularized corneal scar (leukoma) that is associated with the incarceration of iris tissue into the posterior corneal layers. It typically results from a previous full-thickness corneal perforation, where the iris moves forward to plug the defect, subsequently undergoing fibrovascular fusion with the corneal stroma.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Road to Incarceration
content: 1. Full-Thickness Breach: Resulting from trauma or a melting corneal ulcer (desmetocele rupture).
2. Aqueous Outflow: Sudden loss of anterior chamber (AC) depth as aqueous escapes.
3. Iris Prolapse/Plug: The iris is pushed forward by posterior pressure, plugging the corneal hole.
4. Fibrin Scaffolding: Fibrin exudates create a temporary bond between iris and cornea.
5. Fibrosis & Cicatrization: Keratocytes transform into myofibroblasts, creating a permanent collagenous scar (leukoma) that traps the iris tissue.

sections.title: Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Severe reduction in Visual Acuity (if central).
Photophobia and glare (due to light scattering).
Visible white spot on the cornea.
Distorted or 'peaked' pupil shape (corectopia).
Occasional ocular pain if secondary glaucoma is present.
History of trauma or 'bursting' sensation during an infection.

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Slit-Lamp: Dense white opacity, often with superficial or deep vascularization.
Anterior Chamber: Localized shallowing at the site of adherence.
Pupil: Peaked toward the scar; iris pigment may be visible on the posterior scar surface.
IOP: Often elevated due to secondary angle-closure or peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS).
Gonioscopy: Broad-based PAS in the quadrant of the leukoma.

rows: Visualizes iris-cornea interface; measures scar depth.
Gold standard; penetrates opaque tissue to see posterior synechiae.
Quantifies irregular astigmatism and corneal thinning.
Often fails in very dense scars.

sections.title: Red Flags: Immediate Concerns
content: Sudden increase in IOP (Secondary Angle Closure Glaucoma).
Worsening pain and redness (Possible late-onset Endophthalmitis).
Epithelial defect over the scar (Risk of neurotrophic melt).
Deep vascularization reaching the limbus (High risk for graft rejection).

sections.title: Management Strategy Algorithm
content: Step 1: Control IOP using topical Beta-blockers or CAIs (avoid miotics which may pull on synechiae).
Step 2: Assess visual potential via Entoptic visualization or VEP.
Step 3: Medical Management (Lubricants, BCL) for surface irregularities.
Step 4: Surgical Intervention if visual axis is obscured or IOP is refractory.
Step 5: Post-operative monitoring for graft rejection or glaucoma recurrence.

sections.title: Surgical Techniques
content: Internal Synechiolysis: Using viscoelastics (Healon GV) or cyclodialysis spatula via a side-port.
Optical Iridectomy: Creating a new pupil aperture behind clear cornea (if central scar is small).
Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP): Full-thickness graft (indicated for large, central scars).
Sector Iridectomy: Often performed concurrently with PKP to clear the pupillary axis.
Keratoprosthesis (KPro): For bilateral cases or high-risk graft failure (Type 1 Boston KPro).

sections.title: Surgical Complications
content: Intraoperative Iris Hemorrhage (Hyphema).
Iridodialysis during synechiolysis.
High risk of Graft Rejection due to pre-existing vascularization.
Post-keratoplasty Glaucoma (up to 30% of cases).
Endophthalmitis (rare but devastating).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check for a 'double-contoured' scar on AS-OCT to confirm iris involvement.
Pre-operative UBM is essential to plan the site of the donor graft to avoid synechiae recurrence.
Long-term steroid coverage is often needed post-PKP due to the high antigenic load of vascularized scars.
Consider 'Large Diameter PKP' if PAS are extensive to clear the angle.

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations: Peters Anomaly
sections.content: In infants, a central adherent leukoma without a history of trauma is 'Peters Anomaly Type 1' (iris-corneal touch). Unlike acquired leukoma adherent, this is a mesenchymal dysgenesis. Management requires early PKP (within months) to prevent amblyopia, though the prognosis is significantly poorer than in adults.
